graders.evidence:
Reviewed `changelog-check/SKILL.md` (42 lines, no `scripts/`, `references/`, or `evals/` alongside it). No `CLAUDE.md` or authoring style guide exists in this repo, so I reviewed against the generic dimensions only. I treated it as a generic process skill rather than a domain skill — it asserts no external terminology of its own (it defers to "the format that the existing entries use"), so there's nothing for domain sources to contradict, and I skipped domain research.

**Verdict: needs work before shipping.** The prose is genuinely lean and the scope boundary is well drawn, but the skill advertises a capability its frontmatter forbids, and its central mechanic is underspecified.

### Blocking

**1. It promises to write entries but cannot.** `description` (lines 4, 8-9) says it "drafts the entry when it does" and triggers when the user "asks to write the entry for a branch." But `allowed-tools` (line 12) is read-only, and Report (line 37) only says to *quote* the proposed entry. A user who says "write the changelog entry for this branch" loads a skill that can't touch the file. Pick one: add `Edit` to `allowed-tools` and tell the body to insert the entry, or cut "write the entry" from the description and say it proposes text for the user to paste. *(structure/frontmatter)*

**2. Trigger gap on GitHub phrasing.** The description says "merge request" (line 8) only. "Does this PR need a changelog entry" and "pull request" are the more common phrasings and won't match well. Cover both. *(triggering)*

### Important

**3. "The merge base" has no second operand.** Line 23 says to read the diff against the merge base but never names the base branch, so the model guesses between `main`, `master`, `origin/HEAD`, and the upstream tracking branch — and guesses differently across repos. Give the concrete command and the fallback order. *(structure — vague instruction)*

**4. "The changelog file that the repository keeps" (line 23) has no discovery rule.** `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, and fragment-based setups (`changelog.d/`, changesets, towncrier) are all live in the wild, and the fragment case breaks the skill's whole "compare against the changelog lines the branch adds" premise — there is no shared file to diff. State where to look and what to do when the repo uses per-change fragments. *(scope/structure)*

**5. `argument-hint` accepts a merge request; the body doesn't.** Line 11 offers "[branch or merge request]", but line 21 only handles a branch. Nothing says how to resolve an MR/PR number to a branch, and `Bash` is allowed without naming `gh` or `glab`. Either handle the identifier or narrow the hint to a branch. *(frontmatter consistency)*

**6. The description's middle sentence is mechanism, not triggering.** Lines 5-7 ("Reads the diff against the merge base, decides whether... and compares that against...") restate the body's three sections. Descriptions sit in context on every run; this one spends its tokens describing internals the model only needs after loading. Cut to the what plus the "Use when," keep the "Do not use it for release notes" boundary — that one earns its place. *(prose and leanness)*

### Nits

**7. Completion criteria miss a path they created.** Line 41 requires quoting a proposal or naming a covering entry, but line 39 introduces a third outcome: an existing entry that names different behavior than the diff. That case satisfies neither clause. *(structure)*

**8. Line 39's second sentence is justification, not instruction** — "misleads a reader more than a missing entry does" explains why rather than saying what to do. Defensible if you want the model to weight the mismatch heavily; cut it if you want the file lean.

**9. No `evals/`.** Findings 1 and 2 are exactly the kind of thing a trigger eval catches; worth adding before this gets neighbors that overlap it.

---

**Verdict: needs work before shipping.** The prose is genuinely lean and the scope boundary is well drawn, but the skill advertises a capability its frontmatter forbids, and its central mechanic is underspecified.

### Blocking

**1. It promises to write entries but cannot.** `description` (lines 4, 8-9) says it "drafts the entry when it does" and triggers when the user "asks to write the entry for a branch." But `allowed-tools` (line 12) is read-only, and Report (line 37) only says to *quote* the proposed entry. A user who says "write the changelog entry for this branch" loads a skill that can't touch the file. Pick one: add `Edit` to `allowed-tools` and tell the body to insert the entry, or cut "write the entry" from the description and say it proposes text for the user to paste. *(structure/frontmatter)*

**2. Trigger gap on GitHub phrasing.** The description says "merge request" (line 8) only. "Does this PR need a changelog entry" and "pull request" are the more common phrasings and won't match well. Cover both. *(triggering)*

### Important

**3. "The merge base" has no second operand.** Line 23 says to read the diff against the merge base but never names the base branch, so the model guesses between `main`, `master`, `origin/HEAD`, and the upstream tracking branch — and guesses differently across repos. Give the concrete command and the fallback order. *(structure — vague instruction)*

**4. "The changelog file that the repository keeps" (line 23) has no discovery rule.** `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, and fragment-based setups (`changelog.d/`, changesets, towncrier) are all live in the wild, and the fragment case breaks the skill's whole "compare against the changelog lines the branch adds" premise — there is no shared file to diff. State where to look and what to do when the repo uses per-change fragments. *(scope/structure)*

**5. `argument-hint` accepts a merge request; the body doesn't.** Line 11 offers "[branch or merge request]", but line 21 only handles a branch. Nothing says how to resolve an MR/PR number to a branch, and `Bash` is allowed without naming `gh` or `glab`. Either handle the identifier or narrow the hint to a branch. *(frontmatter consistency)*

**6. The description's middle sentence is mechanism, not triggering.** Lines 5-7 ("Reads the diff against the merge base, decides whether... and compares that against...") restate the body's three sections. Descriptions sit in context on every run; this one spends its tokens describing internals the model only needs after loading. Cut to the what plus the "Use when," keep the "Do not use it for release notes" boundary — that one earns its place. *(prose and leanness)*

### Nits

**7. Completion criteria miss a path they created.** Line 41 requires quoting a proposal or naming a covering entry, but line 39 introduces a third outcome: an existing entry that names different behavior than the diff. That case satisfies neither clause. *(structure)*

**8. Line 39's second sentence is justification, not instruction** — "misleads a reader more than a missing entry does" explains why rather than saying what to do. Defensible if you want the model to weight the mismatch heavily; cut it if you want the file lean.

**9. No `evals/`.** Findings 1 and 2 are exactly the kind of thing a trigger eval catches; worth adding before this gets neighbors that overlap it.

---

Want me to apply **(a)** blocking + important (1-6), **(b)** everything, or **(c)** a subset you name? For finding 1 I need your call on direction — read-only proposer, or give it `Edit` and let it write into the changelog.

Note that applying these fixes the file; it does not demonstrate that the skill triggers. Measuring that is an eval run, which is outside this audit.

graders.evidence:
Read it. The prose is unusually clean and the description is well-built — third-person, concrete triggers, and a real anti-trigger ("do not use for whole-version release notes"). The problems are all in the gap between what it promises and what it actually tells the model to do.

## Blocking

**1. The base is never defined (`SKILL.md:23`).** "Read the diff against the merge base" — merge base against *what*? `main`, `master`, `develop`, or the MR's target branch, which is often none of those. This is the one ambiguity that changes the answer: pick the wrong base and the diff contains other people's commits, and the skill reports entries the branch doesn't owe. Name the resolution order (MR target if known → repo default branch via `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` → `main`).

**2. Give the actual commands.** You allowed `Bash` but wrote no git. The two-dot/three-dot distinction bites exactly here: `git diff main..HEAD` is *not* the merge-base diff, `git diff main...HEAD` is. Since the whole skill is premised on merge-base semantics, spell it out:

```
git diff --stat <base>...HEAD
git diff <base>...HEAD -- <changelog path>
```

**3. The comparison step promised in the description is missing from the body.** Line 6 says it "compares that against the changelog lines the branch adds," but the body goes Read → Decide → Report with no step that detects whether the branch touches the changelog at all. Right now "When the branch already carries an entry" (line 39) fires on information the skill was never told to gather. Add that as its own step.

**4. Changelog discovery is hand-waved (`SKILL.md:23`).** "the changelog file that the repository keeps" assumes one exists and that it's a file. Real cases: `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGES.rst`, and fragment directories (`changelog.d/`, towncrier/scriv) where each change is its own new file — for those, "name the section it belongs under" (line 37) doesn't mean anything and the check is "did the branch add a fragment?" Add a discovery step, a note on the fragment-directory shape, and a fallback for when there's no changelog (say so and stop, rather than inventing a format).

**5. The done-condition excludes the "no entry needed" verdict (`SKILL.md:41`).** It requires the report to "either quote a proposed entry or name the existing entry" — but the most common outcome is neither. As written the model can't satisfy it on a pure-refactor branch and will be pushed toward inventing an entry. Add the third branch.

## Worth fixing

**6. Merge requests are in the interface but not in the body.** `argument-hint` and the description both accept an MR (line 7, line 11), but line 21 only says "Take the branch." An MR number or URL has undefined behavior. Either add the resolution (`glab mr view <id>` / `gh pr view <id>` to get source and target branch) or narrow the hint to branches.

**7. "Write the entry" trigger vs. read-only tools.** The description invites "asks to write the entry for a branch" (line 8), but `allowed-tools` has no `Edit`/`Write`. That mismatch is fine if intended — just say so explicitly in Report ("propose the text; do not edit the changelog"), otherwise add `Edit`.

**8. The classifier has no tie-break for the ambiguous middle (`SKILL.md:27-29`).** "Observable without reading the source" cleanly handles endpoints and refactors, but not the cases this will actually hit: performance improvements, changed error messages or log output, deprecation warnings, and *runtime* dependency bumps (line 29 excludes dev-dependency bumps, which implies runtime bumps count, but never says it — and a dep bump carrying a security fix almost always warrants an entry). Add a line: when it's genuinely borderline, say it's borderline and propose an entry — a spurious entry is cheaper than a silent miss, which is the same asymmetry you already argue for in line 39.

**9. `allowed-tools` format (`SKILL.md:12`).** You've used a YAML flow list. The documented form is a comma-separated string — `allowed-tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash`. Worth confirming your loader accepts the list form before shipping; if it doesn't parse, the restriction silently doesn't apply.

The fix that buys the most is #1–#3: without a defined base and a real diff command, every downstream judgment is built on an unspecified input. Want me to apply these?

15	# Changelog Check
16	
17	Decide whether a branch owes the changelog an entry, and draft that entry when it does.
18	
19	## Read the change
20	
21	Take the branch from `$ARGUMENTS`, and default to the current branch.
22	
23	Read the diff against the merge base, and read the changelog file that the repository keeps.
24	
25	## Decide whether the change is user-visible

27	A change is user-visible when a user can observe it without reading the source. That covers a new endpoint, a changed default, a renamed field in a response, a fix for a bug that a user reported, and any break in a public contract.

29	A change is not user-visible when it only moves code, renames a private symbol, edits a test, or bumps a development dependency.

32

# Changelog Check

Decide whether a branch owes the changelog an entry, and draft that entry when it does.

## Read the change

Take the branch from `$ARGUMENTS`, and default to the current branch.

A change is user-visible when a user can observe it without reading the source. That covers a new endpoint, a changed default, a renamed field in a response, a fix for a bug that a user reported, and any break in a public contract.

graders.name: confirms-the-description-states-what-the
graders.evidence:
Read it. The prose is unusually disciplined — the user-visible/not-user-visible split at lines 27–30, the both-kinds tie-break at line 31, and the explicit done condition at line 41 are all better than typical. The problems are all in the same place: **the frontmatter promises three jobs the body only does one of, and the one it does has no commands in it.**

## 1. The core procedure isn't executable (lines 21–23)

This is the big one. `allowed-tools` grants Bash, but the body never names a single command. Three things are left to guess every run:

- **Merge base against what?** Line 23 says "the merge base" as if it's self-evident. `main`, `master`, `develop`, and the MR target branch are all live possibilities. Resolve it explicitly — e.g. read `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, fall back to `main` then `master`, and let the argument override it. Then `git diff $(git merge-base HEAD <base>)...HEAD`.
- **Which changelog?** "the changelog file that the repository keeps" — say how to find it (glob `CHANGELOG*`, `docs/CHANGELOG*`, `changelog.d/` for towncrier-style fragment dirs) and what to do when several match.
- **The branch's own changelog lines.** Your description (line 6) says you compare against "the changelog lines the branch adds," but the body never tells you to diff the changelog separately from the rest. That's the actual comparison the skill exists to make — it should be its own step.

Also add the no-changelog-at-all case. Right now a repo without one sends the skill hunting indefinitely; it should report that and stop.

## 2. Merge requests are advertised but unimplemented

`argument-hint` (line 11) and the description (line 7) both accept a merge request. Line 21 only handles a branch. Nothing resolves an MR ID to its source branch, and nothing uses the MR's *target* branch as the diff base — which for an MR is the correct base, not the repo default. Either add a resolution step (`glab mr view <id>` / `gh pr view <id> --json headRefName,baseRefName`) or cut MRs from the hint and description. Half-support is worse than either.

## 3. "Asks why the changelog check failed" has no procedure (line 8)

That's a diagnostic request — the user has a red CI check and wants to know what tripped it. The body answers a different question: it re-derives a verdict from first principles. If the project's CI enforces its own rule (a required label, a `changelog.d/` fragment, a path-based skip list), your independent verdict can contradict the check and the user is left more confused. Either add a step that reads the check's config before judging, or drop this trigger.

## 4. "Write the entry" vs. read-only tools (lines 8–9, 12)

`allowed-tools` has no Edit or Write, so the skill can only propose — which lines 37 and 41 correctly assume ("quote the entry you propose"). But the trigger phrase "asks to write the entry for a branch" reads as editing the file. A user who says "write my changelog entry" will match this skill and get a quoted block instead. Reword to "asks to draft the entry," or add Edit and give it a step.

## 5. Worth verifying, not certain

- `allowed-tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Bash]` — I'm not confident the YAML-list form parses; the comma-separated string form (`Read, Glob, Grep, Bash`) is what I'd trust. If the list form silently fails to parse, tool gating quietly doesn't apply. Cheap to test before shipping.
- Line 37 says name the section the entry belongs under, but nothing tells you to derive the section names from the existing file. Add that to the read step so it can't invent an `Added:` heading in a changelog that doesn't use them.

## What I'd do

Fixes 1 and 4 are required — the first makes the skill work, the second stops it mis-triggering. For 2 and 3, cutting them from the description is a one-line change and honest; implementing them is real work. If you want to ship today, cut them and add them back when you have the MR-resolution step written.

Want me to apply any of these?

graders.name: does-not-call-the-body-bloated
graders.evidence:
Read it. The prose is unusually disciplined — the user-visible/not-user-visible split at lines 27–30, the both-kinds tie-break at line 31, and the explicit done condition at line 41 are all better than typical. The problems are all in the same place: **the frontmatter promises three jobs the body only does one of, and the one it does has no commands in it.**

## 1. The core procedure isn't executable (lines 21–23)

This is the big one. `allowed-tools` grants Bash, but the body never names a single command. Three things are left to guess every run:

- **Merge base against what?** Line 23 says "the merge base" as if it's self-evident. `main`, `master`, `develop`, and the MR target branch are all live possibilities. Resolve it explicitly — e.g. read `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, fall back to `main` then `master`, and let the argument override it. Then `git diff $(git merge-base HEAD <base>)...HEAD`.
- **Which changelog?** "the changelog file that the repository keeps" — say how to find it (glob `CHANGELOG*`, `docs/CHANGELOG*`, `changelog.d/` for towncrier-style fragment dirs) and what to do when several match.
- **The branch's own changelog lines.** Your description (line 6) says you compare against "the changelog lines the branch adds," but the body never tells you to diff the changelog separately from the rest. That's the actual comparison the skill exists to make — it should be its own step.

Also add the no-changelog-at-all case. Right now a repo without one sends the skill hunting indefinitely; it should report that and stop.

## 2. Merge requests are advertised but unimplemented

`argument-hint` (line 11) and the description (line 7) both accept a merge request. Line 21 only handles a branch. Nothing resolves an MR ID to its source branch, and nothing uses the MR's *target* branch as the diff base — which for an MR is the correct base, not the repo default. Either add a resolution step (`glab mr view <id>` / `gh pr view <id> --json headRefName,baseRefName`) or cut MRs from the hint and description. Half-support is worse than either.

## 3. "Asks why the changelog check failed" has no procedure (line 8)

That's a diagnostic request — the user has a red CI check and wants to know what tripped it. The body answers a different question: it re-derives a verdict from first principles. If the project's CI enforces its own rule (a required label, a `changelog.d/` fragment, a path-based skip list), your independent verdict can contradict the check and the user is left more confused. For 2 and 3, cutting them from the description is a one-line change and honest; implementing them is real work. If you want to ship today, cut them and add them back when you have the MR-resolution step written.

# Changelog Check

Decide whether a branch owes the changelog an entry, and draft that entry when it does.

## Read the change

Take the branch from `$ARGUMENTS`, and default to the current branch.

Read the diff against the merge base, and read the changelog file that the repository keeps.

## Decide whether the change is user-visible

A change is user-visible when a user can observe it without reading the source. That covers a new endpoint, a changed default, a renamed field in a response, a fix for a bug that a user reported, and any break in a public contract.

A change is not user-visible when it only moves code, renames a private symbol, edits a test, or bumps a development dependency.

When one branch carries both kinds, treat the branch as user-visible.

## Report

State the verdict in one line: the branch needs an entry, or it does not.

When it needs one, quote the entry you propose, in the format that the existing entries use, and name the section it belongs under.

When the branch already carries an entry, say whether that entry matches what the diff does. An entry that names a different behavior than the diff misleads a reader more than a missing entry does.

You are done when the report states the verdict, and either quotes a proposed entry or names the existing entry that covers the change.

graders.name: confirms-the-description-states-what-the
graders.evidence:
Read it. The prose is unusually clean — the user-visible/not-visible split and the explicit done-condition are the strongest parts. The problems are all in the gap between what the frontmatter promises and what the body actually tells you to do.

## Blocking

**1. "The merge base" is undefined.** `changelog-check/SKILL.md:23` says to diff against the merge base but never says the merge base *with what*. `main`? `master`? The MR's target branch? Whatever the branch was cut from? On a repo where the default branch isn't obvious, this is the step most likely to silently produce the wrong diff — and a wrong diff means a wrong verdict with no signal that anything went wrong. Name the resolution order explicitly, e.g. the MR target if there is one, otherwise the repo's default branch from `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`.

**2. The merge-request path doesn't exist.** The description (`:7`) and `argument-hint` (`:11`) both advertise merge requests, but the body only ever says "take the branch." Nothing tells you to fetch the MR, resolve it to a branch and a target, or which CLI to use (`gh` vs `glab` — and "merge request" is GitLab vocabulary while nothing mentions `glab`). Either add the fetch-and-resolve step or cut MRs from the description and the argument hint.

**3. "The changelog file that the repository keeps" assumes a shape that many repos don't have.** `:23` doesn't say how to find it, and `:37` ("the section it belongs under") assumes Keep-a-Changelog style. If the repo uses fragment files — towncrier, changesets, `changelog.d/` — the correct entry is a *new file*, not a line under a section, and the skill will confidently propose the wrong artifact. Add a detection step, and say what to do when there's no changelog at all. `Glob` is in `allowed-tools` and never used by the body; this is the step that should use it.

**4. Trigger promises an edit the tools can't perform.** The description lists "asks to write the entry for a branch" as a trigger and says the skill "drafts the entry," but `allowed-tools` (`:12`) has no `Write` or `Edit`, and `:37` only says to *quote* the proposal. Someone who invokes it saying "write the changelog entry" will get a quoted block and no file change. Decide which one you mean, then make the description, the tools, and the report step agree.

## Worth fixing

**5. Bare `Bash` is broader than this skill needs.** It's a read-only analysis skill; scope it to `Bash(git diff:*)`, `Bash(git merge-base:*)`, `Bash(git log:*)`, plus the MR CLI if you keep #2. Unrestricted `Bash` on a skill that only inspects history is a permission prompt you'll get tired of and a blast radius you don't want.

**6. Checking whether the branch already added an entry is never an actual step.** The description says you compare against "the changelog lines the branch adds," and `:39` handles the case, but no step in the body tells you to look. Add it to "Read the change" — restrict the diff to the changelog path — so the `:39` comparison has something to stand on.

**7. Verify `$ARGUMENTS` and `argument-hint` actually work here.** Both are custom-slash-command idioms (`.claude/commands/*.md`). I'm not certain they're substituted/honored in a `SKILL.md`, and I'd rather you test it than take my word. If `$ARGUMENTS` isn't interpolated, `:21` reads as a literal token to the model and the default-to-current-branch behavior is what you'll always get. Phrasing it as "the branch named when the skill was invoked, defaulting to the current branch" is safe either way.

**8. Check the install path.** The file is at `changelog-check/SKILL.md` in the repo root, with nothing else in the repo — no `plugin.json`. Project skills are discovered under `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. As it sits, nothing will load it.

## Gaps in the decision rule

`:27`–`:29` covers the clear cases well, but the ones that actually cause arguments aren't there: performance improvements with no API change, security fixes (often need an entry *and* a CVE reference), reverts, deprecation warnings, and docs-only changes. Two or three more lines would cover the cases where a reviewer would otherwise disagree with the verdict.

One thing I'd leave alone: `:39` ("an entry that names a different behavior than the diff misleads a reader more than a missing entry does") is the best line in the file — it gives the model a reason to prefer, not just a rule to follow.

# Changelog Check

Decide whether a branch owes the changelog an entry, and draft that entry when it does.

## Read the change

Take the branch from `$ARGUMENTS`, and default to the current branch.

Read the diff against the merge base, and read the changelog file that the repository keeps.

## Decide whether the change is user-visible

A change is user-visible when a user can observe it without reading the source. That covers a new endpoint, a changed default, a renamed field in a response, a fix for a bug that a user reported, and any break in a public contract.

A change is not user-visible when it only moves code, renames a private symbol, edits a test, or bumps a development dependency.

When one branch carries both kinds, treat the branch as user-visible.

## Report

State the verdict in one line: the branch needs an entry, or it does not.

When it needs one, quote the entry you propose, in the format that the existing entries use, and name the section it belongs under.

When the branch already carries an entry, say whether that entry matches what the diff does. An entry that names a different behavior than the diff misleads a reader more than a missing entry does.

You are done when the report states the verdict, and either quotes a proposed entry or names the existing entry that covers the change.

# Tune Agent Docs

Whatever agent starts work in a repo reads that repo's AI-steering docs, and often loads several of them into one context window. A root `CLAUDE.md` is rarely the only text an agent takes as instruction. The agent pays a silent tax on every run when these docs disagree. It pays the same tax when they use different words for one thing, bury their point, or demand more rigor than the task needs. This skill treats every steering doc in the repo as one corpus.

Work in two phases: **critique first, edit second**. Build the full picture, present the findings, and only then touch a file.

## Find the corpus

Use `Glob` for the conventions that a harness recognizes today. Read `references/steering-formats.md` for the current list, and for the frontmatter and inclusion rules of each format. The conventions start with `CLAUDE.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md`, including nested per-directory copies and `.claude/rules/**/*.md`. They continue with `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.cursor/rules/**/*.mdc`, and `.cursorrules`. They finish with `.clinerules` or `.clinerules/**/*.md`, `.windsurfrules` or `.windsurf/rules/**/*.md`, `.devin/rules/**/*.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`, and `.kiro/steering/**/*.md`. Where a harness has a local or gitignored variant, include it next to its checked-in counterpart. That pair is a common duplication site, so include both files.

Then follow every pointer that a doc in the corpus makes to another markdown file. A pointer is a "See `docs/x.md` for..." link, an `@import`, or a relative link in a "Where things are" or "further reading" section. A steering doc that tells the agent to consult another file delegates its steering to that file, whether or not the target matches a convention. Pull the target in without asking, because the pointer is the corpus doc that vouches for it.

Then sweep the remaining `.md` files in the repo. Look for files that read as agent-directed but match no known convention and no pointer. The signs are imperative language addressed to "you", "the agent", or "Claude", and frontmatter with an inclusion-like key. List every candidate that this sweep finds. Put the full list to the user with `AskUserQuestion` before you fold any of it in. Do not shorten the list to the files you are unsure about and read the rest in silence. The user decides the scope. An unfamiliar file that turns out to be a changelog or a design doc must not get graded as steering prose.

Read every file in the corpus in full, including every file that a pointer pulled in. A line count or a partial skim is not a read, because the findings live in how these docs relate to each other.

## Load the lenses

- **The standards**: find the authoring conventions that govern this corpus. Look for a `CLAUDE.md`, a `CONTRIBUTING.md`, a docs style guide, a skill-authoring style guide, or an equivalent file. Apply them to every doc in the corpus, not only to the docs they were written for. A repo that holds its `SKILL.md` files to a standard holds its `AGENTS.md` to the same one. A convention the repo settled is settled, so do not raise it as a finding. Take the conventions only from the repo under review. Another repo's `CLAUDE.md` that sits in your context governs its own scope, and so do the user's global conventions.
- **Cross-harness format knowledge**: `references/steering-formats.md` holds the frontmatter fields, the inclusion or scoping mechanism, and the size guidance for each recognized format, taken from the documentation of each vendor. It also holds format-agnostic principles from Anthropic's Skill authoring guidance. Read it once per review. These formats change, so never rebuild the list from memory.

## What to check

- **Token budget**: this is the largest lever a steering doc has over what an agent pays before it does real work, so check it first. Compare the length of each doc against the ceiling of its own format in `references/steering-formats.md`. The ceiling is 200 lines for `CLAUDE.md`, 500 lines for `SKILL.md`, and a per-character cap for Windsurf. A doc under its ceiling is a starting point, not a pass. Length costs tokens whatever its cause, so every line in a short doc still owes a justification against the checks below. Then find content that loads unconditionally through `alwaysApply: true`, `inclusion: always`, or an unscoped `.claude/rules/*.md`, and that matters for one file type or directory alone. Such content belongs in the conditional-loading mechanism of the harness. A doc split into Claude Code `@import` statements is easier to navigate but the same size, because imports still load in full. Never count that split as a token-budget fix.
- **Duplication**: one meaning, one home. Compare guidance by what it *means*, not by string match. Two docs that say one thing in different words duplicate it as fully as two that say it word for word. Paraphrase is the common case, because different hands wrote the docs at different times. The same defect runs inside a single doc, where one rule restated three sections apart reads as three rules. Compare each checked-in doc against its local counterpart. Duplication pays its token cost twice today, and it becomes a contradiction the day one copy gets edited. Prefer one canonical doc plus a pointer or an import over a second copy. Put the surviving copy at the narrowest scope that still covers everywhere the guidance applies. Where a restatement is one idea circled three times, the repair is often a single word that the model already carries priors for. Repeat that word as a term instead of re-explaining the idea in a sentence.
- **No-ops**: an instruction the model already follows by default changes nothing and still costs context every session. Examples are "write clean code", "follow best practices", "be careful when editing files", and "think before you change things". Steering docs collect these because adding a line feels free. Test each sentence on its own against one question: does an agent that never saw this doc behave differently? Judge sentence by sentence, not section by section, because a live section carries dead sentences. When a sentence fails the test, delete the sentence. Do not rewrite it tighter. A reworded no-op is still a no-op, and the reach for a rewrite is what leaves these docs long. Cut hard here. This is usually the largest single cut available.
- **Structural fit per harness**: once a token-budget or leanness finding calls for a split or a narrower scope, judge the fix against what the format itself supports, per `references/steering-formats.md`. The available mechanisms are a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a glob-scoped `.mdc` rule, and a Kiro `fileMatch` steering file. Where the harness has no such mechanism, report the size as a leanness finding instead of recommending a mechanism the harness cannot use. Also flag content that is a multi-step procedure rather than a standing fact. An always-loaded doc holds what is true every session. A workflow belongs in a skill that loads on demand, or in a path-scoped rule.
- **Consistent terminology**: across the whole corpus, one role, tool, or convention carries one name. Hunt synonym drift, such as `the agent` against `Claude` against `the assistant`, `skill` against `capability` against `workflow`, and `worktree` against `workspace`. A term used two ways inside one doc is the same defect at a smaller scale.
- **Front-loading**: each instruction must open on its actionable verb or keyword, with no throat-clearing in front of it. This check reaches past `description` fields. A bullet, a header, or a frontmatter `description` that leads with context before the directive makes a skimming agent miss the point. It also weakens the retrieval match of the harness. Keep this check separate from the *leading word* in the Leitwort sense, which is a compact pretrained concept that the agent thinks with. That belongs to the duplication repair above.
- **Degrees of freedom**: match the specificity of each instruction to how fragile the thing it governs is. An exact, low-freedom script constrains an agent that needs to reason about a judgment call. Loose, high-freedom prose invites improvisation around an exact operation that must run in order.
- **Negation**: a prohibition names the banned behavior into the agent's context, where it competes with the ban. A doc built from `never`, `do not`, and `MUST NOT` walls must state the behavior it wants instead. Keep a prohibition for a guardrail that has no positive phrasing, and pair even that one with what to do in its place.
- **Leanness and staleness**: cut what the agent can derive by reading the codebase itself, such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews. Keep what it cannot derive, such as pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from the defaults of the tool. This cut differs from the no-op check: a derivable fact is true but free to look up, and a no-op is behavior the model already has. Flag time-boxed conditionals such as "until the migration finishes, do X", because they go stale in silence. A dated fold or an old-patterns section ages better than a conditional that still sounds live.
- **Frontmatter validity**: check the frontmatter of each doc against the real schema of its format. Three examples of a violation follow. The first is a Kiro `inclusion` value outside `always`, `fileMatch`, and `manual`. The second is a Cursor `.mdc` file that omits the field its activation mode depends on. The third is a `SKILL.md` `name` that breaks the character or charset limit.

## Resolve conflicts by scope, not by asking

When two docs give contradictory guidance for one thing, resolve it the way these harnesses layer context at runtime. The doc scoped to the narrower area wins for the area it covers, over a repo-wide doc that always loads. A narrower doc is a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a rule scoped by `fileMatch` or `paths`, or a glob-scoped `.mdc` file. Fall back to `AskUserQuestion` only when both sides sit at the same scope and precedence gives no signal. That case is a real tie, not a shortcut around judgment.

## Present findings, then apply

Open with a one-line verdict. Then list the findings ranked by severity, not grouped by check:

- **Blocking**: an active contradiction between docs, an instruction that will make the agent do the wrong thing, or a doc past a hard format limit. Past a hard limit, such as a Windsurf character cap, the tail is truncated in silence and never loads.
- **Important**: terminology drift, a buried directive, or a no-op instruction. It also covers an oversized or always-loaded doc that its harness can scope, and one meaning kept in two places or restated inside one doc. It covers a prohibition wall with no positive target, miscalibrated degrees of freedom, and a convention violation.
- **Nit**: cosmetic polish.

Tag each finding with its dimension, its exact file, and its line. Then offer to apply the findings. Offer three choices: every blocking and important finding, everything, or a subset the user picks. Edit the files directly. A terminology fix or a front-loading fix must land in every occurrence in every file of the corpus. A partial rename leaves the corpus less consistent than before.

## Before you finish

Re-read the diff as a skeptical teammate, and look for these six errors:

- A rename that missed a nested `CLAUDE.md` or a nested rule file.
- A degrees-of-freedom fix that overcorrected into the opposite miscalibration.
- A "contradiction" that was two docs correctly scoped to different areas, now wrongly collapsed into one.
- A scoping fix that narrowed the `paths`, `globs`, or `fileMatchPattern` of a rule past the areas that need it. The agent then stops seeing guidance it relies on.
- A no-op that got reworded instead of deleted, so the finding was reported and the line survived.

graders.name: flags-claude-md-as-exceeding-the
graders.evidence:
Done. `CLAUDE.md` went from 209 lines to 55.

**What survived:** commands, coding conventions, and all four pitfalls — the content an agent cannot derive by reading the code.

**What moved:** `docs/deploying.md` (21 steps verbatim, including "do not skip a step") and `docs/onboarding.md` (setup, db reset, vault path). Both are procedures, not standing facts, so they were costing you 41 lines on every unrelated task. `CLAUDE.md` points to each.

**What was cut:** directory layout, dependency list, architecture prose, FAQ, glossary. Before deleting the architecture section I pulled its two real constraints into conventions — one-way layering, and "long-running work publishes a Celery task" — since neither is visible from a directory listing.

**`CLAUDE.local.md`** dropped to the two lines that are actually local; its build-command block was a verbatim copy of `CLAUDE.md`. I also added a `.gitignore` with `CLAUDE.local.md`, since the repo had none and your personal Postgres port was on track to be committed.

Two things to confirm:

- **The repository layer.** Your architecture section said "services depend on repositories," but the directory layout listed no repository package anywhere. I wrote the surviving rule as "from routers to services to data access" so it doesn't send an agent off to build a layer that may not exist. If there really is a repositories layer, say so and I'll name it precisely — that's better guidance than the generic phrasing.
- **I graded the docs, not the code.** `bloated-claude-md/` contains only the two markdown files in this checkout — no `src/`, no `Makefile`. So I checked the docs for internal consistency and against format guidance, but I could not verify that any command, path, or convention matches the real repo. Worth a quick pass on your end against the actual tree.

# Tune Agent Docs

Whatever agent starts work in a repo reads that repo's AI-steering docs, and often loads several of them into one context window. A root `CLAUDE.md` is rarely the only text an agent takes as instruction. The agent pays a silent tax on every run when these docs disagree. It pays the same tax when they use different words for one thing, bury their point, or demand more rigor than the task needs. This skill treats every steering doc in the repo as one corpus.

Work in two phases: **critique first, edit second**. Build the full picture, present the findings, and only then touch a file.

## Find the corpus

Use `Glob` for the conventions that a harness recognizes today. Read `references/steering-formats.md` for the current list, and for the frontmatter and inclusion rules of each format. The conventions start with `CLAUDE.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md`, including nested per-directory copies and `.claude/rules/**/*.md`. They continue with `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.cursor/rules/**/*.mdc`, and `.cursorrules`. They finish with `.clinerules` or `.clinerules/**/*.md`, `.windsurfrules` or `.windsurf/rules/**/*.md`, `.devin/rules/**/*.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`, and `.kiro/steering/**/*.md`. Where a harness has a local or gitignored variant, include it next to its checked-in counterpart. That pair is a common duplication site, so include both files.

Then follow every pointer that a doc in the corpus makes to another markdown file. A pointer is a "See `docs/x.md` for..." link, an `@import`, or a relative link in a "Where things are" or "further reading" section. A steering doc that tells the agent to consult another file delegates its steering to that file, whether or not the target matches a convention. Pull the target in without asking, because the pointer is the corpus doc that vouches for it.

Then sweep the remaining `.md` files in the repo. Look for files that read as agent-directed but match no known convention and no pointer. The signs are imperative language addressed to "you", "the agent", or "Claude", and frontmatter with an inclusion-like key. List every candidate that this sweep finds. Put the full list to the user with `AskUserQuestion` before you fold any of it in. Do not shorten the list to the files you are unsure about and read the rest in silence. The user decides the scope. An unfamiliar file that turns out to be a changelog or a design doc must not get graded as steering prose.

Read every file in the corpus in full, including every file that a pointer pulled in. A line count or a partial skim is not a read, because the findings live in how these docs relate to each other.

## Load the lenses

- **The standards**: find the authoring conventions that govern this corpus. Look for a `CLAUDE.md`, a `CONTRIBUTING.md`, a docs style guide, a skill-authoring style guide, or an equivalent file. Apply them to every doc in the corpus, not only to the docs they were written for. A repo that holds its `SKILL.md` files to a standard holds its `AGENTS.md` to the same one. A convention the repo settled is settled, so do not raise it as a finding. Take the conventions only from the repo under review. Another repo's `CLAUDE.md` that sits in your context governs its own scope, and so do the user's global conventions.
- **Cross-harness format knowledge**: `references/steering-formats.md` holds the frontmatter fields, the inclusion or scoping mechanism, and the size guidance for each recognized format, taken from the documentation of each vendor. ## What to check

- **Token budget**: this is the largest lever a steering doc has over what an agent pays before it does real work, so check it first. Compare the length of each doc against the ceiling of its own format in `references/steering-formats.md`. The ceiling is 200 lines for `CLAUDE.md`, 500 lines for `SKILL.md`, and a per-character cap for Windsurf. A doc under its ceiling is a starting point, not a pass. Length costs tokens whatever its cause, so every line in a short doc still owes a justification against the checks below. Then find content that loads unconditionally through `alwaysApply: true`, `inclusion: always`, or an unscoped `.claude/rules/*.md`, and that matters for one file type or directory alone. Such content belongs in the conditional-loading mechanism of the harness. A doc split into Claude Code `@import` statements is easier to navigate but the same size, because imports still load in full. Never count that split as a token-budget fix.
- **Duplication**: one meaning, one home. Compare guidance by what it *means*, not by string match. Two docs that say one thing in different words duplicate it as fully as two that say it word for word. Paraphrase is the common case, because different hands wrote the docs at different times. The same defect runs inside a single doc, where one rule restated three sections apart reads as three rules. Compare each checked-in doc against its local counterpart. Duplication pays its token cost twice today, and it becomes a contradiction the day one copy gets edited. Prefer one canonical doc plus a pointer or an import over a second copy. Put the surviving copy at the narrowest scope that still covers everywhere the guidance applies. Where a restatement is one idea circled three times, the repair is often a single word that the model already carries priors for. Repeat that word as a term instead of re-explaining the idea in a sentence.
- **No-ops**: an instruction the model already follows by default changes nothing and still costs context every session. Examples are "write clean code", "follow best practices", "be careful when editing files", and "think before you change things". Steering docs collect these because adding a line feels free. Test each sentence on its own against one question: does an agent that never saw this doc behave differently? Judge sentence by sentence, not section by section, because a live section carries dead sentences. When a sentence fails the test, delete the sentence. Do not rewrite it tighter. A reworded no-op is still a no-op, and the reach for a rewrite is what leaves these docs long. Cut hard here. This is usually the largest single cut available.
- **Structural fit per harness**: once a token-budget or leanness finding calls for a split or a narrower scope, judge the fix against what the format itself supports, per `references/steering-formats.md`. The available mechanisms are a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a glob-scoped `.mdc` rule, and a Kiro `fileMatch` steering file. Where the harness has no such mechanism, report the size as a leanness finding instead of recommending a mechanism the harness cannot use. Also flag content that is a multi-step procedure rather than a standing fact. An always-loaded doc holds what is true every session. A workflow belongs in a skill that loads on demand, or in a path-scoped rule.
- **Consistent terminology**: across the whole corpus, one role, tool, or convention carries one name. Hunt synonym drift, such as `the agent` against `Claude` against `the assistant`, `skill` against `capability` against `workflow`, and `worktree` against `workspace`. A term used two ways inside one doc is the same defect at a smaller scale.
- **Front-loading**: each instruction must open on its actionable verb or keyword, with no throat-clearing in front of it. This check reaches past `description` fields. A bullet, a header, or a frontmatter `description` that leads with context before the directive makes a skimming agent miss the point. It also weakens the retrieval match of the harness. Keep this check separate from the *leading word* in the Leitwort sense, which is a compact pretrained concept that the agent thinks with. That belongs to the duplication repair above.
- **Degrees of freedom**: match the specificity of each instruction to how fragile the thing it governs is. An exact, low-freedom script constrains an agent that needs to reason about a judgment call. Loose, high-freedom prose invites improvisation around an exact operation that must run in order.
- **Negation**: a prohibition names the banned behavior into the agent's context, where it competes with the ban. A doc built from `never`, `do not`, and `MUST NOT` walls must state the behavior it wants instead. Keep a prohibition for a guardrail that has no positive phrasing, and pair even that one with what to do in its place.
- **Leanness and staleness**: cut what the agent can derive by reading the codebase itself, such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews. Keep what it cannot derive, such as pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from the defaults of the tool. This cut differs from the no-op check: a derivable fact is true but free to look up, and a no-op is behavior the model already has. Flag time-boxed conditionals such as "until the migration finishes, do X", because they go stale in silence. A dated fold or an old-patterns section ages better than a conditional that still sounds live.
- **Frontmatter validity**: check the frontmatter of each doc against the real schema of its format. Three examples of a violation follow. The first is a Kiro `inclusion` value outside `always`, `fileMatch`, and `manual`. The second is a Cursor `.mdc` file that omits the field its activation mode depends on. The third is a `SKILL.md` `name` that breaks the character or charset limit.

## Resolve conflicts by scope, not by asking

When two docs give contradictory guidance for one thing, resolve it the way these harnesses layer context at runtime. The doc scoped to the narrower area wins for the area it covers, over a repo-wide doc that always loads. A narrower doc is a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a rule scoped by `fileMatch` or `paths`, or a glob-scoped `.mdc` file. Fall back to `AskUserQuestion` only when both sides sit at the same scope and precedence gives no signal. That case is a real tie, not a shortcut around judgment.

## Present findings, then apply

Open with a one-line verdict. Then list the findings ranked by severity, not grouped by check:

- **Blocking**: an active contradiction between docs, an instruction that will make the agent do the wrong thing, or a doc past a hard format limit. Past a hard limit, such as a Windsurf character cap, the tail is truncated in silence and never loads.
- **Important**: terminology drift, a buried directive, or a no-op instruction. It also covers an oversized or always-loaded doc that its harness can scope, and one meaning kept in two places or restated inside one doc. It covers a prohibition wall with no positive target, miscalibrated degrees of freedom, and a convention violation.
- **Nit**: cosmetic polish.

Tag each finding with its dimension, its exact file, and its line. Then offer to apply the findings. Offer three choices: every blocking and important finding, everything, or a subset the user picks. Edit the files directly. A terminology fix or a front-loading fix must land in every occurrence in every file of the corpus. A partial rename leaves the corpus less consistent than before.

## Before you finish

Re-read the diff as a skeptical teammate, and look for these six errors:

- A rename that missed a nested `CLAUDE.md` or a nested rule file.
- A degrees-of-freedom fix that overcorrected into the opposite miscalibration.
- A "contradiction" that was two docs correctly scoped to different areas, now wrongly collapsed into one.
- A scoping fix that narrowed the `paths`, `globs`, or `fileMatchPattern` of a rule past the areas that need it. The agent then stops seeing guidance it relies on.
- A no-op that got reworded instead of deleted, so the finding was reported and the line survived.
- A paraphrase collapsed onto the broader of the two docs, so the surviving copy now applies where the guidance never did.

# Tune Agent Docs

Whatever agent starts work in a repo reads that repo's AI-steering docs, and often loads several of them into one context window. A root `CLAUDE.md` is rarely the only text an agent takes as instruction. The agent pays a silent tax on every run when these docs disagree. It pays the same tax when they use different words for one thing, bury their point, or demand more rigor than the task needs. This skill treats every steering doc in the repo as one corpus.

Work in two phases: **critique first, edit second**. Build the full picture, present the findings, and only then touch a file.

## Find the corpus

Use `Glob` for the conventions that a harness recognizes today. Read `references/steering-formats.md` for the current list, and for the frontmatter and inclusion rules of each format. The conventions start with `CLAUDE.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md`, including nested per-directory copies and `.claude/rules/**/*.md`. They continue with `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.cursor/rules/**/*.mdc`, and `.cursorrules`. They finish with `.clinerules` or `.clinerules/**/*.md`, `.windsurfrules` or `.windsurf/rules/**/*.md`, `.devin/rules/**/*.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`, and `.kiro/steering/**/*.md`. Where a harness has a local or gitignored variant, include it next to its checked-in counterpart. That pair is a common duplication site, so include both files.

Then follow every pointer that a doc in the corpus makes to another markdown file. A pointer is a "See `docs/x.md` for..." link, an `@import`, or a relative link in a "Where things are" or "further reading" section. A steering doc that tells the agent to consult another file delegates its steering to that file, whether or not the target matches a convention. Pull the target in without asking, because the pointer is the corpus doc that vouches for it.

Then sweep the remaining `.md` files in the repo. Look for files that read as agent-directed but match no known convention and no pointer. The signs are imperative language addressed to "you", "the agent", or "Claude", and frontmatter with an inclusion-like key. List every candidate that this sweep finds. Put the full list to the user with `AskUserQuestion` before you fold any of it in. Do not shorten the list to the files you are unsure about and read the rest in silence. The user decides the scope. An unfamiliar file that turns out to be a changelog or a design doc must not get graded as steering prose.

Read every file in the corpus in full, including every file that a pointer pulled in. A line count or a partial skim is not a read, because the findings live in how these docs relate to each other.

## Load the lenses

- **The standards**: find the authoring conventions that govern this corpus. Look for a `CLAUDE.md`, a `CONTRIBUTING.md`, a docs style guide, a skill-authoring style guide, or an equivalent file. Apply them to every doc in the corpus, not only to the docs they were written for. A repo that holds its `SKILL.md` files to a standard holds its `AGENTS.md` to the same one. A convention the repo settled is settled, so do not raise it as a finding. Take the conventions only from the repo under review. Another repo's `CLAUDE.md` that sits in your context governs its own scope, and so do the user's global conventions.
- **Cross-harness format knowledge**: `references/steering-formats.md` holds the frontmatter fields, the inclusion or scoping mechanism, and the size guidance for each recognized format, taken from the documentation of each vendor. It also holds format-agnostic principles from Anthropic's Skill authoring guidance. Read it once per review. These formats change, so never rebuild the list from memory.

## What to check

- **Token budget**: this is the largest lever a steering doc has over what an agent pays before it does real work, so check it first. Compare the length of each doc against the ceiling of its own format in `references/steering-formats.md`. The ceiling is 200 lines for `CLAUDE.md`, 500 lines for `SKILL.md`, and a per-character cap for Windsurf. A doc under its ceiling is a starting point, not a pass. Length costs tokens whatever its cause, so every line in a short doc still owes a justification against the checks below. Then find content that loads unconditionally through `alwaysApply: true`, `inclusion: always`, or an unscoped `.claude/rules/*.md`, and that matters for one file type or directory alone. Such content belongs in the conditional-loading mechanism of the harness. A doc split into Claude Code `@import` statements is easier to navigate but the same size, because imports still load in full. Never count that split as a token-budget fix.
- **Duplication**: one meaning, one home. Compare guidance by what it *means*, not by string match. Two docs that say one thing in different words duplicate it as fully as two that say it word for word. Paraphrase is the common case, because different hands wrote the docs at different times. The same defect runs inside a single doc, where one rule restated three sections apart reads as three rules. Compare each checked-in doc against its local counterpart. Duplication pays its token cost twice today, and it becomes a contradiction the day one copy gets edited. Prefer one canonical doc plus a pointer or an import over a second copy. Put the surviving copy at the narrowest scope that still covers everywhere the guidance applies. Where a restatement is one idea circled three times, the repair is often a single word that the model already carries priors for. Repeat that word as a term instead of re-explaining the idea in a sentence.
- **No-ops**: an instruction the model already follows by default changes nothing and still costs context every session. Examples are "write clean code", "follow best practices", "be careful when editing files", and "think before you change things". Steering docs collect these because adding a line feels free. Test each sentence on its own against one question: does an agent that never saw this doc behave differently? Judge sentence by sentence, not section by section, because a live section carries dead sentences. When a sentence fails the test, delete the sentence. Do not rewrite it tighter. A reworded no-op is still a no-op, and the reach for a rewrite is what leaves these docs long. Cut hard here. This is usually the largest single cut available.
- **Structural fit per harness**: once a token-budget or leanness finding calls for a split or a narrower scope, judge the fix against what the format itself supports, per `references/steering-formats.md`. The available mechanisms are a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a glob-scoped `.mdc` rule, and a Kiro `fileMatch` steering file. Where the harness has no such mechanism, report the size as a leanness finding instead of recommending a mechanism the harness cannot use. Also flag content that is a multi-step procedure rather than a standing fact. An always-loaded doc holds what is true every session. A workflow belongs in a skill that loads on demand, or in a path-scoped rule.
- **Consistent terminology**: across the whole corpus, one role, tool, or convention carries one name. Hunt synonym drift, such as `the agent` against `Claude` against `the assistant`, `skill` against `capability` against `workflow`, and `worktree` against `workspace`. A term used two ways inside one doc is the same defect at a smaller scale.
- **Front-loading**: each instruction must open on its actionable verb or keyword, with no throat-clearing in front of it. This check reaches past `description` fields. A bullet, a header, or a frontmatter `description` that leads with context before the directive makes a skimming agent miss the point. It also weakens the retrieval match of the harness. Keep this check separate from the *leading word* in the Leitwort sense, which is a compact pretrained concept that the agent thinks with. That belongs to the duplication repair above.
- **Degrees of freedom**: match the specificity of each instruction to how fragile the thing it governs is. An exact, low-freedom script constrains an agent that needs to reason about a judgment call. Loose, high-freedom prose invites improvisation around an exact operation that must run in order.
- **Negation**: a prohibition names the banned behavior into the agent's context, where it competes with the ban. A doc built from `never`, `do not`, and `MUST NOT` walls must state the behavior it wants instead. Keep a prohibition for a guardrail that has no positive phrasing, and pair even that one with what to do in its place.
- **Leanness and staleness**: cut what the agent can derive by reading the codebase itself, such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews. Keep what it cannot derive, such as pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from the defaults of the tool. This cut differs from the no-op check: a derivable fact is true but free to look up, and a no-op is behavior the model already has. Flag time-boxed conditionals such as "until the migration finishes, do X", because they go stale in silence. A dated fold or an old-patterns section ages better than a conditional that still sounds live.
- **Frontmatter validity**: check the frontmatter of each doc against the real schema of its format. Three examples of a violation follow. The first is a Kiro `inclusion` value outside `always`, `fileMatch`, and `manual`. The second is a Cursor `.mdc` file that omits the field its activation mode depends on. The third is a `SKILL.md` `name` that breaks the character or charset limit.

## Resolve conflicts by scope, not by asking

When two docs give contradictory guidance for one thing, resolve it the way these harnesses layer context at runtime. The doc scoped to the narrower area wins for the area it covers, over a repo-wide doc that always loads. A narrower doc is a nested `CLAUDE.md`, a rule scoped by `fileMatch` or `paths`, or a glob-scoped `.mdc` file. Fall back to `AskUserQuestion` only when both sides sit at the same scope and precedence gives no signal. That case is a real tie, not a shortcut around judgment.

## Present findings, then apply

Open with a one-line verdict. Then list the findings ranked by severity, not grouped by check:

- **Blocking**: an active contradiction between docs, an instruction that will make the agent do the wrong thing, or a doc past a hard format limit. Past a hard limit, such as a Windsurf character cap, the tail is truncated in silence and never loads.
- **Important**: terminology drift, a buried directive, or a no-op instruction. It also covers an oversized or always-loaded doc that its harness can scope, and one meaning kept in two places or restated inside one doc. It covers a prohibition wall with no positive target, miscalibrated degrees of freedom, and a convention violation.
- **Nit**: cosmetic polish.

Tag each finding with its dimension, its exact file, and its line. Then offer to apply the findings. Offer three choices: every blocking and important finding, everything, or a subset the user picks. Edit the files directly. A terminology fix or a front-loading fix must land in every occurrence in every file of the corpus. A partial rename leaves the corpus less consistent than before.

## Before you finish

Re-read the diff as a skeptical teammate, and look for these six errors:

- A rename that missed a nested `CLAUDE.md` or a nested rule file.
- A degrees-of-freedom fix that overcorrected into the opposite miscalibration.
- A "contradiction" that was two docs correctly scoped to different areas, now wrongly collapsed into one.
- A scoping fix that narrowed the `paths`, `globs`, or `fileMatchPattern` of a rule past the areas that need it. The agent then stops seeing guidance it relies on.
- A no-op that got reworded instead of deleted, so the finding was reported and the line survived.
- A paraphrase collapsed onto the broader of the two docs, so the surviving copy now applies where the guidance never did.

- Two systems coexist: the legacy single `.windsurfrules` file, and the newer `.windsurf/rules/` directory of scoped markdown files.
- The size limits are hard. A global rules file caps at roughly 6,000 characters. A single workspace rule file caps at roughly 12,000 characters. A file over the limit does not raise an error. It is truncated in silence.
- Source: [thepromptshelf.dev, .windsurfrules guide](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/windsurfrules-complete-guide-2026/)

## Cline: `.clinerules`, `.clinerules/*.md`

- A single `.clinerules` file fits a small setup. A larger project splits into a `.clinerules/` directory of topic files with conditional loading.
- Cline sets no hard limit, but adherence degrades in practice beyond roughly 300 lines. The recommended ceiling for reliable behavior is about 150 lines.
- Source: [thepromptshelf.dev, Cline rules guide](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/cline-rules-complete-guide-2026/)

## GitHub Copilot: `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md`

- `copilot-instructions.md` is a single repo-wide file with no inclusion-mode frontmatter. Every instruction in it applies everywhere, all the time.
- `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` files are separate documents with their own frontmatter, scoped to matching files. Review them as their own corpus members. Do not fold them into the findings of the repo-wide file. The repo-wide file and a scoped companion that covers the same ground form a duplication site, like any other pair in this corpus.

Meridian is a multi-tenant billing platform: FastAPI over Postgres, Stripe for payments, Celery for
async work.

## Build and test commands

- `make install` installs the Python dependencies into `.venv`.
- `make build` compiles the protobuf stubs and builds the Docker image.
- `make test` runs the unit suite with `pytest -q`. Use this while iterating.
- `make test-integration` runs the integration suite against the docker-compose stack. It starts a
  real Postgres and Redis, so run it before you push rather than on every change.
- `make lint` runs `ruff check .` and `black --check .`.
- `make seed` loads the demo tenant into the local Postgres.
- Run a single test by node id: `pytest tests/unit/billing/test_tax.py::test_vat`.

## Coding conventions

- Format with `black`, line length 100. The repo overrides the default of 88, so an editor left on
  the default reformats every line it touches and fails CI.
- Type-annotate every function signature. `mypy --strict` runs in CI and blocks the merge.
- Service functions take a `Session` as their first argument. They never open their own session.
- Money is `Decimal` everywhere, never `float`. Amounts cross the Stripe boundary as integer cents.
- Timestamps are timezone-aware UTC `datetime` objects. Naive datetimes fail validation.
- Every ORM model carries a `tenant_id` column, and every query filters on it.
- Raise `MeridianError` subclasses, never bare `Exception`. The error handler maps them to status
  codes by class.
- Routers depend on services, services depend on repositories, and repositories depend on the
  database. Nothing depends upwards, which keeps the business logic testable without an HTTP client.
- Work that outlives a request goes to a Celery task, published by the service module. Five failed
  attempts land the task in the dead-letter queue.
- Test files mirror the source tree, so `src/billing/tax.py` is tested by
  `tests/unit/billing/test_tax.py`.

## Pitfalls

- **Stripe webhook signature ordering.** Verify the signature against the raw request body before
  any middleware parses it. FastAPI re-serializes the JSON with different key order and whitespace,
  and the recomputed signature then never matches. Read the body with `await request.body()` as the
  first statement in the handler.
- **Enum migration transaction flag.** Postgres cannot run `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` inside a
  transaction block. Any migration that adds a value to an enum must set
  `transaction_per_migration = False` in its Alembic revision, or it fails on deploy and leaves the
  revision table half-applied.
- **Redis TTL dedup.** The webhook dedup key TTL must stay above 72 hours, because Stripe retries a
  failed webhook for three days. A shorter TTL lets a retry through as a fresh event and charges
  the customer twice.
- **Fixture customer UUID.** The customer UUID in `tests/fixtures/customers.py` is registered in the
  shared Stripe test account. Changing it breaks every integration test that touches payments, and
  the failure reads as a network error rather than a bad fixture.
- **Migration conflicts.** "Target database is not up to date" means someone merged a migration
  after you branched. Rebase on `main` and rerun `alembic upgrade head`.

## Ownership

- The platform team owns `deploy/chart`. Open a ticket for changes there.
- Staging credentials live in the shared vault under `meridian/staging`.

To release, follow every step in `docs/deploying.md`. New to the repo? `docs/onboarding.md`.

# Deploy Meridian

Follow every step in order, including for a one-line change. The steps are exact because a skipped
verification ships an unverified image to production.

1. Check that `main` is green in CI.
2. Run `scripts/changelog.py` to draft the release notes.
3. Open the release notes and edit the summary line.
4. Tag the commit with `git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "release vX.Y.Z"`.
5. Push the tag with `git push origin vX.Y.Z`.
6. Wait for the release pipeline to build and push the image.
7. Confirm the image digest in the pipeline log matches the tag.
8. Run `helm diff upgrade meridian deploy/chart -f deploy/staging.yaml`.
9. Read the diff and confirm no unexpected resource is replaced.
10. Run `helm upgrade meridian deploy/chart -f deploy/staging.yaml`.
11. Watch the staging rollout with `kubectl rollout status deploy/meridian`.
12. Run the smoke suite with `scripts/smoke.py --env staging`.
13. Check the staging error rate on the Grafana dashboard for ten minutes.
14. Announce the production deploy in `#meridian-releases`.
15. Run `helm diff upgrade meridian deploy/chart -f deploy/prod.yaml`.
16. Run `helm upgrade meridian deploy/chart -f deploy/prod.yaml`.
17. Watch the production rollout with `kubectl rollout status deploy/meridian`.
18. Run `scripts/smoke.py --env prod`.
19. Watch the error rate and the p99 latency for thirty minutes.
20. If either regresses, run `helm rollback meridian` and page the on-call engineer.
21. Close the release ticket and paste the dashboard screenshot into it.

graders.evidence:
CLAUDE.md went from 209 lines to 52; CLAUDE.local.md from 18 to 6.

**Kept in full** — the two sections that actually change behavior and can't be inferred: coding conventions (line length 100, `Decimal` money, `tenant_id` on every query, `MeridianError`) and all four pitfalls. Both now sit near the top instead of at line 134.

**Cut outright:**
- **Directory layout** (28 lines) — Claude can list the tree faster than it can read a description of it, and a stale layout section actively misleads. The one non-obvious part, the strict layering direction, survives as a bullet.
- **Dependency list** (22 lines) — duplicates the lockfile, and will drift out of sync with it.
- **Architecture prose** — mostly a generic description of three-tier web apps. The two load-bearing rules (layering, no long work in requests) are now bullets.
- **Duplicated command block in CLAUDE.local.md** — identical to CLAUDE.md, so it was pure token cost.
- **Opening "read all of it before you touch anything"** — instructions to read the instructions don't help.

**Moved, not deleted** (I didn't want to throw away things a human wrote): onboarding → `docs/onboarding.md`, the 21-step release runbook → `docs/deploying.md`, glossary → `docs/glossary.md`. The FAQ got split — the four answers that were real troubleshooting went into `docs/onboarding.md`, and the ones that just restated a convention ("Can I use `float`?") were dropped since the convention itself is still there.

Two things worth your judgment:

- **The glossary.** Most of those 19 terms are standard billing vocabulary a model already knows, so it was costing context for nothing. But if newer teammates lean on it, `docs/glossary.md` is the better home anyway.
- **`docs/` didn't exist.** The old layout section claimed it did, so I created it. If long-form docs actually live in a wiki, move these three files there and update the pointers at the bottom of CLAUDE.md.

One thing I couldn't check: since the directory has no source tree, I took every factual claim — make targets, file paths, the pitfalls — at face value. If any were already stale, they're still stale, just shorter.

134	## Coding conventions
135	
136	- Format with `black`, line length 100. The default of 88 is not what this repo uses.
137	- Type-annotate every function signature. `mypy --strict` runs in CI and blocks the merge.
138	- Service functions take a `Session` as their first argument. They never open their own session.
139	- Money is `Decimal` everywhere, never `float`. Amounts cross the Stripe boundary as integer cents.
140	- Timestamps are timezone-aware UTC `datetime` objects. Naive datetimes fail validation.
141	- Every ORM model carries a `tenant_id` column, and every query filters on it.
142	- Raise `MeridianError` subclasses, never bare `Exception`. The error handler maps them to status
143	  codes by class.
144	- Test files mirror the source tree, so `src/billing/tax.py` is tested by `tests/unit/billing/test_tax.py`.

146	## Pitfalls
147	
148	- **Stripe webhook signature ordering.** Verify the signature against the raw request body before
149	  any middleware parses it. FastAPI re-serializes the JSON with different key order and whitespace,
150	  and the recomputed signature then never matches. Read the body with `await request.body()` as the
151	  first statement in the handler.
152	- **Enum migration transaction flag.** Postgres cannot run `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` inside a
153	  transaction block. Any migration that adds a value to an enum must set
154	  `transaction_per_migration = False` in its Alembic revision, or it fails on deploy and leaves the
155	  revision table half-applied.
156	- **Redis TTL dedup.** The webhook dedup key TTL must stay above 72 hours, because Stripe retries a
157	  failed webhook for three days. A shorter TTL lets a retry through as a fresh event and charges
158	  the customer twice.
159	- **Fixture customer UUID.** The customer UUID in `tests/fixtures/customers.py` is registered in the
160	  shared Stripe test account. Changing it breaks every integration test that touches payments, and
161	  the failure reads as a network error rather than a bad fixture.

164	
165	**Why is the test suite slow?** The integration suite starts a real Postgres and a real Redis. Run
166	`make test` alone while you iterate, and run the integration suite before you push.

170

172

188	## Glossary
189	
190	- **Tenant** - one customer organization. Every row in the database belongs to exactly one tenant.
191	- **Account** - a user inside a tenant.
192	- **Subscription** - a recurring plan that a tenant holds.
193	- **Proration** - the partial charge that a mid-cycle plan change produces.
194	- **Invoice** - the monthly statement that a subscription generates.
195	- **Charge** - one Stripe payment attempt against an invoice.
196	- **Refund** - a reversal of a charge, whole or partial.
197	- **Dunning** - the retry sequence that runs after a failed charge.
198	- **Entitlement** - a feature flag that a plan grants to a tenant.
199	- **Seat** - one billable user inside a subscription.
200	- **Grace period** - the days a tenant keeps access after a failed payment.
201	- **Plan** - the priced template that a subscription instantiates.
202	- **Cycle** - the billing period that an invoice covers.
203	- **Credit note** - a negative invoice line that offsets an earlier charge.
204	- **Webhook event** - one message that Stripe delivers to `src/payments/webhooks.py`.
205	- **Idempotency key** - the token that makes a repeated Stripe call safe.
206	- **Demo tenant** - the tenant that `make seed` loads into the local database.
207	- **Dead-letter queue** - where a Celery task lands after five failed attempts.
208	- **Smoke suite** - the short post-deploy check in `scripts/smoke.py`.
